draft.text:
When the stability data for our fourteenth production batch arrived from our manufacturer, the pH readings were lower than our baseline by approximately 0.4 units.

A difference of 0.4 units sounds minor - and the batch is not unsafe - but it is enough to alter the behaviour of our emollient blend. The texture feels slightly different, in a way that I think our customers would notice. Because of this, we are holding the entire batch.

When we traced the discrepancy back through the documentation, we found the cause. Our raw material supplier had modified their preservative blend to a more acidic system. They had sent a revised specification sheet three months ago, but it was buried in our records.

I am writing about this because it illustrates a common vulnerability in cosmetic manufacturing. There is a general assumption that reordering the same formula from the same supplier yields an identical product. It often does not.

I am not suggesting the supplier acted in bad faith. They did issue the updated documentation, but because the change was not actively flagged, it went unnoticed until we ran our own tests.

If you do not compare the Certificate of Analysis - the CoA - for every incoming batch against your original baseline, these shifts remain invisible. The first person to notice the difference will likely be the customer. For us, avoiding that outcome is worth the cost of holding a batch.
